endorsements.quote: Engage with clinical stakeholders early in the clinical process, and working from problem to solution with earnest evaluation of whether a particular method—or machine learning at all—is most appropriate to address the problem.

Engage with clinical stakeholders early in the clinical process, and working from problem to solution with earnest evaluation of whether a particular method—or machine learning at all—is most appropriate to address the problem.
Evaluate machine learning solutions against already existing methods used in relevant healthcare settings as well as simple non-machine learning baselines.
Establish institutional monitoring teams and processes for the longitudinal assessment and adjustment of clinical models for issues such as dataset shift.
Evaluate models in the local context of their intended deployment, recognizing that performance can be sensitive to subtle specifics.
Dedicate increased focus to the techniques of transfer learning and local fine-tuning when necessary.
Engage in subgroup analysis of the outputs of all MLHC projects, in order to understand and engage in dialogue and remediation regarding relevant disparities.
Develop and hold projects to explicit standards regarding fairness, equity, and maximally permissible performance disparities between demographic groups.
Monitor performance after deployment to identify the presence of dataset shift and help inform decisions about when model re-training is needed.
Utilize standardized model reporting techniques, such as “Model Cards” [ 82 ] in order to ensure that model training contexts, targeted uses, and limitations are clearly disclosed.
Engage clinicians, nurses, patients, and other end-users of systems in order to understand how model outputs are understood, and how their presentation can be optimized.

Provide detailed dataset descriptions (such as those described in “Datasheets for Datasets” [ 72 , 73 ]) that inform data harmonization practices, especially when the data use is different from its original intended use.
Validate clinical targets and metrics via clinical trials focused on tangible patient-relevant endpoints such as mortality or disability reduction.
Establish processes for ongoing monitoring of clinician feedback, ensuring that the practical usability of models is continuously optimized.
Offer rewards for long-lived, successful deployments of MLHC projects, as well as terminating projects assessed to have harms or negative impacts.
Establish guidelines and checklists to update and/or retrain models [ 123 ] in response to changing data and process environments.
Work to generate standardized adversarial assessments [ 122 ] to probe the vulnerabilities of a given clinical model.
Focus the creation of novel datasets on rectifying existing issues of patient underrepresentation.
Actively invite patient and caregiver stakeholders into all levels of the process, ensuring that procedures and outputs are aligned with tangible patient needs.

unlisted_practices: Ensure that appropriate backup procedures are in place to recognize and respond to model downtime or performance deterioration.
Continue training clinicians for model-free circumstances to avoid deskilling.
Require regulators to mandate clear establishment of model limitations and communicate them to health systems and end users.
Share data cleaning and preprocessing code alongside model development code, with performance breakdowns for data subgroups.
Prioritize prediction of objective or patient-centered outcomes rather than agreement with clinician assessments alone.
Incorporate fairness constraints into model training processes rather than as after-the-fact correction.
Promote FAIR datasets and privacy-preserving data sharing to broaden access to health data.
Establish industry standards for responsible AI development incorporating patient-centric and ethical values.
Use implementation frameworks such as RE-AIM to plan real-world adaptation of ML initiatives.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/narrative review paper offering recommendations for stakeholders (researchers, clinicians, institutions, regulators) to reorient machine learning in healthcare from technical novelty to equitable impact.
